<div class="notes">
  <article class="note" id="from-language-to-reliable-control">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-09-09T18:06:06-04:00">9 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">Scaling and physical generalization</h2>
    <p>I suspect the main challenge in scaling embodied intelligence is achieving physical generalization. In language and mathematics, autoregressive models can reuse shared symbolic structures across tasks. Extending this reuse to physical control requires accounting for different dynamics and constraints, including contact and boundary conditions or even different governing partial differential equations. Shared representations, priors and solution strategies may help with these differences, but they do not establish that one control law will transfer reliably across systems.</p>
    <p>Such transfer could come from identifying the operating regime and applying the appropriate local laws, so it need not imply a unified physical theory. I would test this on unfamiliar systems whose relevant dynamics can be inferred from available observations and whose control objectives are feasible. Reliable control across such systems, without extensive reference trajectories or retraining for each system, would suggest a general mechanism for physical reasoning and control synthesis. This sets a broader target than the task and embodiment transfer shown in <a href="https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-robotics-2-brings-whole-body-intelligence-to-robots/">recent vision-language-action demonstrations</a>.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="note" id="emergence-and-physical-intelligence">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-09-07T11:40:00-04:00">7 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
      <span>Ithaca, New York</span>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">Emergence and physical intelligence</h2>
    <p>I do not expect physical intelligence to show the emergence reported for large language models. If a mechanism for wide transfer exists, it should come from structure rather than from parameter count, because the laws that govern a physical system have always turned out to be short.</p>
  </article>
